newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Midwest economy's edge may narrow in 1997.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Midwest economy's edge may narrow in 1997.

text.p: The powerful Midwest economy should roll along at a steady clip in 1997, but its edge over the overall U.S. economy may be narrowing, economists say.
Economists predicted the region's main engine -- its manufacturing base -- will remain strong this year, fueled in part by robust exports.
"The region is expected to continue to operate at a relatively high level of economic activity in 1997," said Diane Swonk, economist with First Chicago NBD.
"There is a sense, however, that we are starting to hit a ceiling in our own backyard," she said. "The premium that we once earned on growth is beginning to narrow," Swonk said.
In recent years, the Midwest economy has outperformed the nation as a whole, but the region's momentum has slowed "as the Midwest bumps its head against the ceiling on economic growth," Swonk said.

She forecast 1997 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in the five-state region -- Illinois, Michigan, Ohio, Indiana and Wisconsin -- at 2.6 percent, only slightly ahead of her growth forecast for the nation of 2.4 percent.

The rest of the country also may be catching up to the Midwest thanks to economic upturns in California and the Northeast, according to Joan Schneider, an economist with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp in Chicago.

She said if the Midwest economy outperforms the rest of the country at all in 1997, it will be by a lesser margin than in past years. "The manufacturing sector is at a fairly high level of activity, but we just don't see the room for them to grow," Schneider said.

The Midwest's economic strength in recent years contrasted sharply with the woes of the early 1980s, when scores of "Rust Belt" factories closed and a flood of Japanese auto imports waylaid the U.S. auto industry, a key engine of the regional economy.
As recently as 1994 the Midwest's GDP grew by 4.1 percent, outpacing U.S. GDP growth of 3.5 percent, Swonk said.
But economists say there are other risks threatening the Midwest's string of economic successes, notably a shortage of workers and a strengthening dollar.
Swonk cited the region's unemployment rate at a 23-year low of 4.5 percent last year, and a shrinking pool of skilled workers.
"My main concern for the near term is the labor market conditions here; they're very tight," agreed Asha Bangalore, an economist with Northern Trust in Chicago. "We might see some wage pressures."
And the strengthening dollar, in theory, could thwart U.S. exports that are critical to Midwest industries such as autos, manufacturing and agriculture.
But Swonk said economic recoveries in Latin America should diminish the risk posed by a strong dollar.

"The Big Three (automakers) are concerned about the dollar because they would like to export more aggressively to Japan, but it's unclear to me that the dollar plays the same role that it did in the past given the overwhelming majority of our trade is now shifting to partners that the yen and the mark don't matter to," Swonk said.
